name: Iris
lede: Iris is the blue-violet of the flower named for the Greek rainbow goddess; in the Middle Ages the same plant also gave painters a green, which is stranger than it sounds.

sections.title: A rainbow, a flower and an eye
sections.body:
*Iris* was the Greek messenger of the gods, and the word came to mean the rainbow as well [1]. Paterson's dictionary of color gives the color word as the reddish-blue of the iris flower, with the rainbow as a second sense, and records an old name for the same dark blue, *flag* [1]. The yellow iris has a color word of its own, *flambé*, which Paterson glosses simply as the yellow of that flower [1]. Ovid pictures the goddess putting on a robe of a thousand colors and drawing an arc across the sky, and Jarman quotes the passage [6].

The eye's iris is a separate use of the word. It is the ring in front of the lens that forms the pupil and widens or narrows it with the light [8]. Its color comes from the pigment melanin [1]. Birren points out something that surprises many readers: practically all mammals, humans included, are born with blue eyes, and the blue is scattered light in an unpigmented iris, not a blue pigment [8].

In the flower's own world, medieval flower symbolism read the iris as protection and prosperity, according to Pastoureau [5]. In his garden poem, Jarman lists a purple iris among the colors present there [6].

sections.title: The flower as a color standard
sections.body: Naturalists used the petal as a measuring stick. In Baty's account of Werner's nomenclature, as expanded by Syme in 1821, the standard called Pale Blackish Purple is shown beside the inner petals of an iris, drawn in a Dutch plant book of 1865 [11]. The pairing is a reminder that a flower can be a reference color as well as a decoration.

sections.title: Iris green
sections.body:
By the fourteenth century painters were looking for alternatives to verdigris, a copper green that was popular but unpredictable and that could eat through the parchment it was painted on [3]. Two plant colors filled the gap, sap green and iris green [3]. Ball describes iris green as the juice of iris flowers mixed with water, possibly with alum as a thickener, and used for manuscript illumination [3].

The Pigment Compendium adds detail [2]. Medieval manuscripts name flower juices as a source of green, sometimes confusingly called sap green [2]. Iris green could be made up as a *pezzetta*, a piece of linen dipped in the juice and dried, or by squeezing the flowers and mixing the juice with an alum base [2]. A specific source named in the literature is *Iris germanica*, whose leaves contain the yellow compound mangiferin [2]. Thompson speculated in 1956 that the main coloring matter of iris green is probably chlorophyll [2]. Italian recipes also call it lily green, or *verde giglio*; the recipes describe the flowers as purple, which suggests that the lilies in question were irises [2].

Books disagree on the source. Paterson defines iris green as a medieval dye made from the leaves of buckthorn, or possibly from iris flowers, while Ball and the Compendium name the iris flower first [1][3][2]. The Compendium notes a related blending of names: a nineteenth-century edition of Field's *Chromatography* mentions blue iris flowers being added to sap green, and malachite itself has been called iris green [2]. Ball adds a limit: these meadow juices suited a monk's manuscript page, but they were too fragile for large altarpiece work [3].

sections.title: Iris blue
sections.body:
The blue is harder to pin down. The Compendium finds iris blue in three medieval manuscripts, but Thompson wrote in 1935 that a way of making it may have been known without being generally practiced [2]. One Florentine manuscript says the secret is to take the yellow parts out of the flowers, which probably means the pollen [2]. A compendium of recipes of 1808 also lists it [2].

By the nineteenth century the term had drifted. Field in 1835 used *iris blue* as a synonym for blue bice, a name applied mainly to azurite but also to blue verditer [2]. St Clair writes of the "iris-blue" glass of Chartres and Saint-Denis, tying it to cobalt, so the name was still serving as a color description for something that no flower made [9].

sections.title: The swatch is a modern blue-violet
sections.body:
The swatch on this page, #6258C4, comes from three modern lists [7]. The 1955 ISCC-NBS system places it in block 185 as a strong purplish blue [7]. The Maerz and Paul dictionary of 1930 has it too, and our library dates that entry to 1916; the xkcd color survey of 2010 adds it as well [7]. Its Munsell value, computed by our library, is 9.0PB 4.3/14.6, a mid-dark blue-violet with strong chroma [7].

A different color shares the first word. xkcd's "Iris purple" is #AC1DB8, a hot magenta-leaning purple, and our core list files it under its own name, [[iris-purple]] [7]. The nearest neighbors of the swatch are [[dark-periwinkle]] and [[abbey]], with [[royal-blue]] about nine units away [7]. Paterson gives the flower both a blue-violet and a yellow, so no single swatch can stand for it [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
The color is rare in paint. In our archive of 23,781 museum paintings, a color within ten CIEDE2000 units of this swatch covers at least 2 per cent of the canvas in 14 works, as photographed [10]. Six of the 14 are from the 1900s, a rate about six times the archive's average, and two are Norwegian, in a country that makes up only 120 paintings of the archive [10].

The largest area is Matisse's [[painting:commons-Q1853880|Blue Nude IV]] of 1952, where the color covers about a quarter of the canvas, followed by Jawlensky's *Red Path, St. Prex* of 1915 and Munch's [[painting:commons-Q18889878|Forest on the Way to Borre]] of 1901 [10]. The earliest match is Bronzino's portrait of Bia de' Medici, from 1543, where the color covers about 8 per cent [10]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, so read them as screen colors, not as pigment tests [10].

The word itself is old and steady in print. In Google Books the adjective use, which is the color sense, peaks in the 1870s [12]. Among the named colors in our archive count, it is rarer than 86 per cent of them [12]. To see the color's source, look at the inner petals of a bearded iris, where the plate of 1865 placed its darkest standard [11].

questions.q: True or false: a newborn's blue eyes come from a blue pigment in the iris.
Why did medieval painters turn to plant greens such as sap green and iris green?
choices: Verdigris was popular but unpredictable and could damage parchment
Plant greens were more lightfast than any mineral
questions.answer: Verdigris was popular but unpredictable and could damage parchment

questions.q: What does the name Iris mean in Greek mythology?
choices: The rainbow goddess and messenger of the gods
The goddess of the night sky
questions.answer: The rainbow goddess and messenger of the gods

openers: A flower once gave painters a green: iris green, made from the juice of iris flowers.
Babies' blue eyes contain no blue pigment; the color of a newborn's iris is scattered light.
Syme's Werner nomenclature pairs the standard Pale Blackish Purple with the inner petals of an iris.
